comments.author: @Emacee1701
comments.text: You left out a very important element in Detroit becoming the motor city.  In the 19th century, Michigan was already the center of vehicle product - horse-drawn vehicles.  Instead of iron ore, the makers of wagons, coaches and carriages drew on Michigan's then-abundant forests.  And the expertise developed in making horse-drawn vehicles was the basis for making motorized vehicles.  The Durant-Dort Carriage Company of Flint, a leading maker of horse drawn vehicles, became General Motors.  Along they way, GM acquired Fisher Brothers, another carriage maker, and GM cars were advertised as "body by Fisher."  It wasn't just a "choke-point" that made Detroit the "Motor City," it was the established companies already there.  PS:  Random Olds was not from Detroit.  He was from Lansing.  The Oldsmobile Division stayed in Lansing until GM closed it down.  Buick and Chevrolet remain in Flint, where it all began.

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: That’s fair, and while I did touch on the preexisting machinists and supplier network in the video, your carriage-industry point adds useful detail to why that expertise was already concentrated there.

comments.author: @jeffbranch8072
comments.text: Specifically on the economic graph the lines of floating iron ore downstream vs. pushing coal upstream cross at Detroit, making Detroit the lowest cost point to locate industry requiring both. This concept was explained to me by my supervisor at the time, Bob Szudarek, when he was working to publish his 1996 book, 'How Detroit Became the Automotive Capital'. And also as implied in this video Bob explained the talent pool in Detroit, quite a few of whom served together in the Spanish-American War. Before automobiles Detroit was already the world's largest manufacturer of railcars and cast iron stoves. Detroit was not the world leader in cigars but as the "Havana of the North" it was a major player. Lumber baron money was readily available to invest in new companies since they didn't trust New York City with this money.
